questionPapers.title: Paper 3 (Set C): Subqueries, CTEs, Window Functions & Analytical SQL
questionPapers.subtitle: Covers ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, LAG/LEAD, Common Table Expressions & Subqueries

questions.topic: Window Functions: ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK
questions.questionText: If three employees tie for the highest salary (100k), what rank numbers are assigned to the subsequent employee (90k) by ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), and DENSE_RANK() respectively?
options: ROW_NUMBER assigns 4, RANK assigns 2, DENSE_RANK assigns 4
ROW_NUMBER assigns 2, RANK assigns 4, DENSE_RANK assigns 2
ROW_NUMBER assigns 4, RANK assigns 4, DENSE_RANK assigns 2
ROW_NUMBER assigns 1, RANK assigns 2, DENSE_RANK assigns 3
questions.explanation: For tied top 3 values (100k): ROW_NUMBER yields unique sequence [1, 2, 3] so next is 4. RANK yields [1, 1, 1] and skips positions, assigning 4 to next. DENSE_RANK yields [1, 1, 1] without gaps, assigning 2 to next.

questions.topic: PARTITION BY vs ORDER BY in OVER Clause
questions.questionText: What is the purpose of the PARTITION BY clause inside a window function OVER() specification?
options: It divides result set rows into separate partition groups across which the window function evaluates independently
It restricts the query to return only 1 row per department
It deletes duplicate rows in each department
It sorts the final query output by department ID
questions.explanation: PARTITION BY divides the input rowset into partitions. The window function is computed independently for each partition, preserving all original detail rows in the final output.

questions.questionText: What does the LAG(sales_amount, 1) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date) window function return for a given row?
options: The maximum sales_amount in the table
The sales_amount of the immediately preceding row in chronological order (or NULL for the first row)
The sales_amount of the subsequent row in chronological order
The average sales_amount of all previous rows combined
questions.explanation: LAG(col, offset) accesses data from a preceding row at a specified physical offset prior to the current position within the window partition.

questions.questionText: What is a primary architectural benefit of Common Table Expressions (WITH clause) compared to deeply nested subqueries?
options: CTEs improve code readability, modularity, and can be referenced multiple times within the same parent statement
CTEs are stored permanently on disk as physical tables
CTEs disable transaction logging to make queries run 100x faster
CTEs automatically create primary keys on all CTE columns
questions.explanation: CTEs provide a clean named temporary result set defined using WITH that improves SQL readability, modular structure, and reusability within a single execution.

questions.questionText: What two SELECT queries must be combined with UNION ALL inside a Recursive CTE (WITH RECURSIVE)?
questions.codeSnippet:
WITH RECURSIVE org_tree AS (
    -- Query 1
    SELECT emp_id, manager_id, name FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
    UNION ALL
    -- Query 2
    SELECT e.emp_id, e.manager_id, e.name 
    FROM employees e JOIN org_tree t ON e.manager_id = t.emp_id
)
SELECT * FROM org_tree;
options: The Anchor Member (initial base case) and the Recursive Member (referencing the CTE name)
The Update query and the Delete query
The Primary Key query and the Foreign Key query
The Aggregate query and the Grouping query
questions.explanation: A Recursive CTE requires an Anchor Member (base non-recursive query) UNION ALLed with a Recursive Member that references the CTE itself until recursion terminates.

questions.questionText: Why can correlated subqueries exhibit poor performance ($O(N^2)$ time complexity) on large datasets?
questions.codeSnippet:
SELECT * FROM orders o 
WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = o.customer_id);
options: Correlated subqueries lock the entire database server on every row read
The subquery references outer query column values ('o.customer_id') and must be re-evaluated once for EVERY candidate row processed by the outer query
Correlated subqueries disable all indexes on the outer table
Correlated subqueries convert all integers into floating point numbers
questions.explanation: A correlated subquery relies on outer query values. Conceptual evaluation requires executing the subquery once per candidate row of the outer table unless optimized to a join by the query optimizer.

questions.questionText: Which statement accurately describes the evaluation behavior of EXISTS (subquery)?
questions.codeSnippet: SELECT name FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);
options: EXISTS requires the subquery to return all table columns
EXISTS returns true as soon as the subquery yields at least one matching row, short-circuiting further evaluation for that outer row
EXISTS calculates the total sum of all rows returned by the subquery
EXISTS returns false if the subquery contains any NULL values
questions.explanation: EXISTS tests for row existence. As soon as the subquery produces a single matching row, EXISTS short-circuits to TRUE without scanning remaining subquery rows for that outer record.

questions.questionText: Why does the query 'WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM employees)' return zero rows if ANY manager_id in the subquery is NULL?
options: The SQL engine crashes when encountering NULL in IN lists
Subqueries are not allowed inside NOT IN clauses
NOT IN requires all column data types to be fixed-width CHAR
NOT IN with a list containing NULL evaluates to 'NOT (id = val1 OR id = NULL)', which resolves to UNKNOWN (false) for every row
questions.explanation: If the subquery result contains NULL, 'x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL)' expands to '(x != 1 AND x != 2 AND x != NULL)'. Since 'x != NULL' is UNKNOWN, the whole AND condition evaluates to UNKNOWN, returning 0 rows. NOT EXISTS avoids this trap.

questions.questionText: What syntax requirement is mandatory when using a subquery in the FROM clause (Derived Table)?
questions.codeSnippet: SELECT avg_salary FROM (SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id) AS dept_summary;
options: The derived subquery MUST be assigned a table alias (e.g. 'AS dept_summary')
The subquery cannot contain GROUP BY clauses
The outer query must use a UNION operator
The subquery must contain a WHERE clause
questions.explanation: ANSI SQL requires subqueries in the FROM clause (derived tables) to have an explicit table alias so that outer SELECT expressions can reference its columns.

questions.questionText: Which window function specification correctly calculates a cumulative running total of 'amount' sorted by 'order_date'?
options: SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
CUMULATIVE_SUM(amount) BY order_date
SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY amount)
TOTAL(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date)
questions.explanation: SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) accumulates values from the first row of the partition up to the current row.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between ROWS BETWEEN and RANGE BETWEEN in SQL window frames?
options: ROWS operates on physical row offsets; RANGE operates on logical value offsets of the ORDER BY column (treating duplicate values as a single peer group)
ROWS works only on text columns; RANGE works only on integer columns
There is no difference; ROWS and RANGE produce identical results for tied values
ROWS requires a GROUP BY clause; RANGE requires a HAVING clause
questions.explanation: ROWS defines window frame bounds based on physical row counts (e.g., 2 rows before). RANGE defines bounds based on value ranges of the ORDER BY key, grouping duplicate peer values together.

questions.questionText: Why does LAST_VALUE(salary) OVER (ORDER BY hire_date) return the CURRENT row's salary instead of the last salary in the partition unless frame bounds are modified?
options: LAST_VALUE is a deprecated function that behaves like FIRST_VALUE
LAST_VALUE works only when salary is indexed
LAST_VALUE evaluates in reverse alphabetical order
Default window frame with ORDER BY is 'RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW', capping the frame at the current row
questions.explanation: The default window frame when ORDER BY is supplied is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. Thus the 'last' value in the frame is the current row. To get the true partition end, use 'ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING'.

questions.questionText: What does NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY test_score DESC) do when applied to 100 student exam scores?
options: Returns only students whose score ends in 4
Divides the ordered score records into 4 equal quartiles (1 to 4), assigning 1 to top 25% students and 4 to bottom 25%
Multiplies each student score by 4
Calculates 4th degree polynomial averages
questions.explanation: NTILE(n) divides an ordered partition into 'n' roughly equal buckets (quartiles for 4, percentiles for 100), assigning bucket numbers 1 through n.

questions.topic: ANY / SOME vs ALL Subquery Comparison
questions.questionText: What condition makes 'WHERE salary > ALL (SELECT salary FROM employees WHERE dept_id = 5)' evaluate to true?
options: The candidate salary must match at least one salary in department 5
The candidate salary must be equal to the average salary in department 5
The candidate salary must be greater than the MINIMUM salary in department 5
The candidate salary must be greater than the MAXIMUM salary in department 5
questions.explanation: '> ALL (subquery)' requires the value to be strictly greater than EVERY value returned by the subquery (i.e. greater than the maximum value).

questions.questionText: What error occurs if a subquery placed in the SELECT column list returns 2 rows instead of 1 row?
questions.codeSnippet: SELECT name, (SELECT order_id FROM orders WHERE customer_id = c.id) FROM customers c;
options: Division by zero error
Infinite loop timeout
Subquery returns more than 1 row (Scalar Subquery Violation)
Table deadlock exception
questions.explanation: A subquery placed where a single scalar value is expected (such as in the SELECT column expression list) must return at most 1 row and 1 column. Returning multiple rows causes a runtime scalar subquery error.

questions.questionText: How are multiple CTEs declared within a single WITH statement?
options: Using UNION ALL between CTE blocks
Separated by semicolons
Repeating the WITH keyword for every CTE definition
Comma-separated list under a single WITH keyword
questions.explanation: Multiple CTEs are defined sequentially separated by commas following a single WITH keyword. Subsequent CTEs can reference previously defined CTEs.

questions.questionText: Where are window functions allowed to be placed in a SQL query block?
options: Only in WHERE and HAVING clauses
Window functions can be placed anywhere without restriction
Only in SELECT and ORDER BY clauses (NOT in WHERE or HAVING clauses directly)
Only in FROM and GROUP BY clauses
questions.explanation: Window functions execute AFTER WHERE, GROUP BY, and HAVING phases. Therefore, they are allowed only in the SELECT list and ORDER BY clause. To filter by a window function result, wrap it in a CTE or derived table.

questions.questionText: Which window frame specification computes a 3-day moving average (current day plus 2 preceding days)?
options: AVG(daily_sales) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
SUM(daily_sales) / 3 OVER (PARTITION BY sale_date)
AVG(daily_sales) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND 3 FOLLOWING)
MOVING_AVG(daily_sales, 3)
questions.explanation: 'ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW' includes 3 physical rows in the window frame (2 previous + current), calculating the exact 3-period moving average.

questions.questionText: Which pattern correctly fetches the top 2 highest-paid employees inside EACH department?
options: ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 2 PARTITION BY dept_id
SELECT TOP 2 * FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE salary = MAX(salary) GROUP BY dept_id
Using DENSE_RANK() PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC in a CTE, then filtering WHERE rnk <= 2
questions.explanation: The standard SQL pattern for Top-N per group uses DENSE_RANK() or ROW_NUMBER() partitioned by group and ordered by metric, filtered in an outer query or CTE.

questions.questionText: What query pattern retrieves customers who have NEVER placed an order?
options: SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers c WHERE c.id = orders.customer_id;
SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers c INNER JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.id IS NULL;
SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.id IS NULL;
SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers c CROSS JOIN orders o;
questions.explanation: The Anti-Join pattern performs a LEFT JOIN from customers to orders and filters 'WHERE orders.id IS NULL', isolating customer records with zero matching orders.

questions.questionText: Which SQL query pattern correlates rows within the same table to compare events or calculate intervals between consecutive user interactions?
questions.codeSnippet:
SELECT 
    a.user_id,
    a.login_time AS current_login,
    b.login_time AS previous_login
FROM user_logins a
JOIN user_logins b 
  ON a.user_id = b.user_id AND a.login_id = b.login_id + 1;
options: Self JOIN
CROSS JOIN
FULL OUTER JOIN
NATURAL JOIN
questions.explanation: A Self JOIN joins a table to itself using aliases (e.g., `a` and `b`), allowing row-to-row comparisons within the same dataset.

questions.questionText: What is the critical behavioral difference between `COUNT(*)` and `COUNT(status)` when analyzing a table where 5 out of 10 rows have a NULL status?
questions.codeSnippet:
-- Table has 10 total rows (5 have NULL status)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_rows, COUNT(status) AS status_count FROM orders;
options: COUNT(*) returns 5 and COUNT(status) returns 10
COUNT(*) returns 10 (all rows), while COUNT(status) returns 5 (ignores NULLs)
Both queries return 10
COUNT(status) raises an error when encountering NULL values
questions.explanation: `COUNT(*)` counts all rows in the dataset regardless of content. `COUNT(column_name)` counts only non-NULL occurrences in that specific column.

questions.questionText: When creating a database Trigger to write audit log entries whenever a user's email address is updated, which timing and event specification should be defined?
questions.codeSnippet:
CREATE TRIGGER audit_user_email_update
AFTER UPDATE OF email ON users
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO email_audit_log(user_id, old_email, new_email, updated_at)
    VALUES (OLD.id, OLD.email, NEW.email, DATETIME('now'));
END;
options: BEFORE DELETE ON users
BEFORE INSERT ON users
INSTEAD OF SELECT ON users
AFTER UPDATE OF email ON users FOR EACH ROW
questions.explanation: An `AFTER UPDATE OF email ON users FOR EACH ROW` trigger executes after an update statement finishes, exposing `OLD.email` (previous value) and `NEW.email` (updated value) for audit records.

questions.questionText: When should a developer choose a Temporary Table (`CREATE TEMP TABLE`) over a Common Table Expression (`WITH cte AS ...`) in a complex multi-step stored procedure?
options: When the intermediate result set is referenced multiple times across separate queries or requires explicit indexing
CTEs cannot perform JOIN operations
Temporary tables are stored permanently on network disk backup drives
CTEs only work inside SQLite
questions.explanation: CTEs are scoped to a single query execution. Temporary tables persist across multiple queries in the session, allowing index creation and repeated references without recomputing data.

questions.questionText: Which SQL clause implements 'Upsert' functionality by updating an existing record if a UNIQUE key conflict occurs during insertion?
questions.codeSnippet:
INSERT INTO user_stats (user_id, login_count)
VALUES (101, 1)
ON CONFLICT(user_id) DO UPDATE SET
    login_count = user_stats.login_count + 1;
options: WHERE DUPLICATE REPLACE
ON CONFLICT(...) DO UPDATE
TRY INSERT CATCH UPDATE
IF EXISTS ALTER
questions.explanation: `INSERT INTO ... ON CONFLICT(key) DO UPDATE SET ...` (standard SQL / PostgreSQL / SQLite) atomizes insertion or updating upon primary key or unique constraint collisions.

questionPapers.studentNamePattern: Candidate first name starting with S, T, U, V, W, X, Y, or Z
questionPapers.title: Paper 4 (Set D): Query Performance Optimization, Indexing, ACID & Transactions
questionPapers.subtitle: Covers B-Tree/Clustered Indexes, ACID Properties, Transaction Isolation Levels, Deadlocks & Triggers

questions.questionText: In a standard B-Tree index structure, what data is stored inside the leaf nodes?
options: Only raw binary hash values of table primary keys
Unordered string text copies of table descriptions
The indexed key values along with pointers/row identifiers (or full row data for clustered index) to locate table records
Transaction log checkpoints
questions.explanation: B-Tree leaf nodes contain sorted index key values paired with row locators (tuple IDs/pointers or clustered row data) allowing logarithmic $O(log N)$ search traversal.

questions.questionText: How does a Clustered Index fundamentally differ from a Non-Clustered Index?
options: A Clustered Index physically dictates the storage order of table data rows on disk (thus only 1 per table); a Non-Clustered Index is a separate structure pointing to table data (multiple per table)
A table can have up to 250 Clustered Indexes and only 1 Non-Clustered Index
Non-Clustered Indexes store physical rows on disk; Clustered Indexes store pointers
Clustered Indexes slow down SELECT queries but speed up INSERTs
questions.explanation: A Clustered Index sorts and stores table data rows physically on disk according to key order (1 per table). A Non-Clustered Index maintains a separate B-Tree structure storing keys and row locators.

questions.questionText: Given a composite index INDEX idx_user_loc (country, state, city), which WHERE clause CANNOT utilize this index effectively?
options: WHERE country = 'USA' AND state = 'CA' AND city = 'San Francisco'
WHERE country = 'USA' AND state = 'CA'
WHERE city = 'San Francisco' AND state = 'CA' (without specifying country)
WHERE country = 'USA'
questions.explanation: Composite B-Tree indexes follow the Left-Prefix Rule. Searches must specify leading index columns ('country'). A query filtering only on 'city' and 'state' skips the leading 'country' column, preventing index lookup.

questions.questionText: In database query execution plans, why is an 'Index Seek' operation preferred over an 'Index Scan'?
options: An Index Seek navigates B-Tree pointer levels directly to pinpoint specific matching rows; an Index Scan reads through the entire index page by page
There is no difference; Seek and Scan are identical operations
An Index Scan uses CPU cache while an Index Seek reads from tape storage
An Index Seek converts tables to XML format
questions.explanation: Index Seek traverses B-Tree branches directly to target specific key values in $O(log N)$ steps. Index Scan inspects every leaf page of the index sequentially ($O(N)$), consuming more I/O.

questions.questionText: What is a 'Covering Index' and why does it eliminate 'Key Lookup / Bookmark Lookup' overhead?
questions.codeSnippet: CREATE INDEX idx_emp_dept_sal ON employees (department_id) INCLUDE (salary, name);
options: It is an index created exclusively on temporary tables
It is an index that covers multiple database instances across network nodes
It is an index that encrypts database passwords
It is an index containing ALL columns required by a query, allowing the database engine to satisfy the query entirely from the index without reading table pages
questions.explanation: A Covering Index contains all columns referenced in SELECT, WHERE, and JOIN clauses of a query. The engine fulfills the request directly from index pages, skipping table page lookups.

questions.questionText: Which ACID property guarantees that once a transaction is committed, its changes persist permanently even in the event of a system crash or power outage?
options: Isolation
Durability
Consistency
Atomicity
questions.explanation: Durability guarantees that once a transaction commits, recorded changes are written to non-volatile transaction logs/disk and survive subsequent system crashes.

questions.questionText: What concurrency anomaly can occur under the READ UNCOMMITTED transaction isolation level?
options: Dirty Reads (reading uncommitted data modifications made by another concurrent transaction that might later roll back)
Lost Updates only
Automatic schema modifications
Strict Serializability enforcement
questions.explanation: READ UNCOMMITTED allows reading dirty (uncommitted) data modified by active concurrent transactions. If the writing transaction rolls back, the reading transaction has acted on invalid data.

questions.questionText: What anomaly occurs when Transaction A reads a row, Transaction B updates and COMMITS that row, and Transaction A re-reads the row obtaining different values?
options: Deadlock Exception
Dirty Read
Non-Repeatable Read (Fuzzy Read)
Phantom Read
questions.explanation: A Non-Repeatable Read occurs under READ COMMITTED when re-reading a row yields updated column values because another transaction committed changes between reads.

questions.questionText: What is a 'Phantom Read' anomaly under the REPEATABLE READ isolation level?
options: A transaction reading its own uncommitted updates
Transaction A executes a range query (e.g. WHERE age > 30), Transaction B INSERTS a new row matching that condition and commits, and Transaction A re-executes the query seeing new 'phantom' rows
Reading data from a deleted database table
An index corrupted by power outage
questions.explanation: Phantom Reads occur when a concurrent transaction inserts new records matching a range query criteria. Re-running the range query in the first transaction reveals newly inserted 'phantom' rows.

questions.questionText: How does the SERIALIZABLE isolation level prevent all transaction concurrency anomalies (Dirty Reads, Non-Repeatable Reads, Phantom Reads)?
options: By converting all relational tables into flat text files
By disabling transaction rollbacks completely
By using range locks or Optimistic Concurrency Control (SSI) to ensure concurrent transaction execution yields results equivalent to executing transactions serially one after another
By enforcing a 1-second sleep delay between every SQL query
questions.explanation: SERIALIZABLE is the highest isolation level. It uses strict range locking or Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) to guarantee execution outcomes match a strict serial sequential ordering.

questions.questionText: What command allows rolling back a portion of a transaction to a specific intermediate checkpoint without discarding the entire transaction?
options: UNDO TO sp1;
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT sp1;
RESTORE CHECKPOINT sp1;
CANCEL STATEMENT sp1;
questions.explanation: SAVEPOINT creates a named marker within a transaction. 'ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT name' undoes modifications executed after that marker while keeping earlier statements intact for COMMIT.

questions.questionText: What action does a SQL Database Engine take when a Deadlock is detected between two concurrent transactions?
options: It chooses one transaction as the 'Deadlock Victim', terminates it, and rolls back its work so the other transaction can complete
It pauses both transactions indefinitely until a user restarts the server
It deletes the tables involved in the deadlock
It merges both transactions into a single combined transaction
questions.explanation: When a deadlock cycle is detected by the lock manager, the database engine selects a transaction (usually the one least costly to undo) as a deadlock victim, aborted with an error so the remaining transaction can proceed.

questions.questionText: Which type of trigger is executed PRIOR to writing data changes to disk, allowing input data validation or transformation?
questions.codeSnippet:
CREATE TRIGGER trg_check_salary
BEFORE INSERT ON employees
FOR EACH ROW
EXECUTE FUNCTION validate_salary();
options: BEFORE Trigger
INSTEAD OF Trigger
AFTER Trigger
EVENT Trigger
questions.explanation: A BEFORE trigger executes prior to committing row modifications, making it ideal for validating constraints, sanitizing input values, or aborting invalid operations before disk write.

questions.questionText: What is a key difference between Stored Procedures and User-Defined Functions (UDFs) in relational SQL databases?
options: Stored Procedures can execute transaction control statements (COMMIT/ROLLBACK) and return multiple result sets; UDFs cannot modify database state or manage transactions
Stored Procedures cannot take input parameters
UDFs can execute DDL commands while Stored Procedures cannot
UDFs are stored on client machines while Stored Procedures store on server
questions.explanation: Stored Procedures can perform full data modification, transaction control (COMMIT/ROLLBACK), and return multiple result sets. Pure SQL Functions (UDFs) are restricted from side-effects like transaction commits.

questions.topic: Execution Plans: Hash Join vs Nested Loop
questions.questionText: When does a Query Optimizer typically choose a Hash Join over a Nested Loop Join?
options: When memory is completely exhausted
When joining two large, unsorted datasets where build and probe hash tables in memory are faster than performing millions of index lookups
When executing queries with NO JOIN conditions
When joining a 5-row table with a 10-row indexed table
questions.explanation: Hash Joins excel at joining large, unsorted datasets. The optimizer builds an in-memory hash table on the smaller input, probing it with rows from the larger input, outperforming nested loops.

questions.questionText: What benefit does a Filtered (Partial) Index provide: 'CREATE INDEX idx_unpaid ON orders(customer_id) WHERE is_paid = false'?
options: Prevents unpaid orders from being updated
Encrypts customer IDs for unpaid orders
Deletes paid orders automatically
Reduces index size and maintenance overhead by indexing ONLY rows that satisfy the WHERE condition (unpaid orders)
questions.explanation: A Filtered / Partial Index indexes a subset of table rows matching a predicate. It saves storage space and index maintenance CPU overhead while accelerating queries filtering on that predicate.

questions.questionText: Which WHERE clause expression is SARGable (Search Argument Able) and can effectively utilize a standard index on 'hire_date'?
options: WHERE DATE_FORMAT(hire_date, '%Y') = '2025'
WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM hire_date) = 2025
WHERE hire_date >= '2025-01-01' AND hire_date < '2026-01-01'
WHERE YEAR(hire_date) = 2025
questions.explanation: Wrapping indexed columns inside functions (e.g. YEAR(hire_date)) renders expressions non-SARGable, forcing full table scans. Using raw column range comparisons ('hire_date >= ...') allows index seeking.

questions.questionText: What is the lock compatibility rule between Shared Locks (S) and Exclusive Locks (X) during concurrent queries?
options: Locks apply only to temporary views
Multiple transactions can hold Shared Locks (S) concurrently on the same row; an Exclusive Lock (X) blocks ALL other Shared and Exclusive locks
Shared Locks block other Shared Locks
Exclusive Locks allow multiple concurrent writers
questions.explanation: Shared (S) locks for reading are mutually compatible. Exclusive (X) locks for writing require exclusive access, blocking all other S and X locks on that resource.

questions.questionText: How can a database optimize case-insensitive search queries like: 'WHERE LOWER(email) = 'user@example.com''?
options: By running ANALYZE TABLE every 5 seconds
By removing the email column from the primary key
By converting the database into a CSV file
By creating an Expression / Function-Based Index: CREATE INDEX idx_lower_email ON users (LOWER(email));
questions.explanation: An Expression / Function-Based index evaluates and indexes computed values (such as LOWER(email)), allowing the query optimizer to perform index seeks for function-wrapped queries.

questions.questionText: Why do enterprise web applications use Database Connection Pools (e.g. PgBouncer, HikariCP)?
options: To reuse a warm cache of established database connections, avoiding the high latency overhead of opening/authenticating TCP sockets on every HTTP request
To automatically compress SQL source code into zip files
To bypass database user password authentication
To store user passwords in local browser storage
questions.explanation: Opening TCP database connections involves expensive SSL/TLS handshakes and process allocations. Connection pooling maintains reusable open connections, dramatically reducing latency.

questions.questionText: How does `DENSE_RANK()` behave differently from `ROW_NUMBER()` when ranking employees with identical salaries?
questions.codeSnippet:
-- Two employees earn $100,000 (tied)
SELECT name, salary,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) as row_num,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) as dense_rk
FROM employees;
options: DENSE_RANK produces floating-point numbers
ROW_NUMBER raises an error on ties
DENSE_RANK skips numbers after ties (1, 1, 3)
ROW_NUMBER assigns distinct sequential numbers (1, 2, 3); DENSE_RANK assigns tied ranks (1, 1, 2) without skipping numbers
questions.explanation: `ROW_NUMBER()` assigns unique sequential integers (1, 2, 3). `DENSE_RANK()` assigns identical ranks to tied values without skipping subsequent rank numbers (1, 1, 2).

questions.questionText: What causes a Deadlock scenario in concurrent relational database transactions, and how is it mitigated?
questions.codeSnippet:
-- Transaction 1: Locks Row A, waits for Row B
-- Transaction 2: Locks Row B, waits for Row A
options: Deadlocks occur when disk space runs out; they are mitigated by clearing logs
Deadlocks occur when two or more transactions hold locks on resources the other requires; mitigated by accessing tables/rows in a consistent deterministic order
Deadlocks are prevented by disabling index locks
Deadlocks occur when foreign keys are deleted
questions.explanation: Deadlocks occur when transactions wait mutually for locks held by each other. Mitigate by acquiring locks in a consistent order and keeping transaction windows short.

questions.questionText: What is the primary performance benefit of Table Partitioning (`PARTITION BY RANGE`) on multi-terabyte transactional tables?
options: Partition Pruning enables the query engine to scan only relevant data partitions, skipping unneeded date ranges entirely
It compresses text columns using ZIP compression
It eliminates the need for primary keys
It converts relational tables into NoSQL document stores
questions.explanation: Partition Pruning excludes non-relevant table partitions from query execution plans based on WHERE filtering (e.g., filtering `sale_date = '2025-04-01'` scans only the Q2 2025 partition).

questions.questionText: Which SQL technique allows calculating multiple conditional metrics in a single SELECT query pass over a dataset?
questions.codeSnippet:
SELECT 
    COUNT(*) AS total_orders,
    SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'Completed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS completed_orders,
    SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'Cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled_orders
FROM orders;
options: Running separate SELECT queries and combining them with UNION
Executing nested cursor loops
Using GROUP BY HAVING on status
Using SUM(CASE WHEN ... END) or FILTER (WHERE ...)
questions.explanation: Combining aggregate functions with CASE statements (or ANSI `FILTER (WHERE ...)`) computes distinct subset counts in a single table scan.

questions.questionText: Why should database administrators always build indexes on Foreign Key columns in relational database schemas?
options: Foreign key indexes automatically encrypt table rows
Indexes convert foreign keys into primary keys
Without an index on Foreign Keys, deleting a row from the parent table can cause a full table lock or full scan on the child table
Foreign Keys cannot be created unless an index already exists
questions.explanation: When modifying parent rows, database engines verify child table constraints. Un-indexed Foreign Key columns force full table scans or share locks on the child table, hindering concurrency.

questions.questionText: When creating a Foreign Key constraint with 'ON DELETE CASCADE', what occurs in the child table when a parent row is deleted?
questions.codeSnippet:
ALTER TABLE order_items
ADD CONSTRAINT fk_orders
FOREIGN KEY (order_id) REFERENCES orders(id)
ON DELETE CASCADE;
options: All matching child rows in 'order_items' are automatically deleted along with the parent order row
The parent order row is deleted, but the child rows remain in 'order_items' as orphaned records
The database engine raises an error and blocks the deletion of the parent order row
The child rows in 'order_items' have their order_id column automatically set to NULL
questions.explanation: ON DELETE CASCADE specifies that when a row in the referenced parent table is deleted, all matching referencing rows in the child table are automatically deleted as well.

questions.questionText: What is the primary operational difference between CHAR(20) and VARCHAR(20) data types in SQL databases?
options: CHAR(20) is a fixed-length string padded with spaces to 20 characters regardless of input length; VARCHAR(20) stores variable length strings up to 20 characters plus a length byte
CHAR(20) allows storing up to 20 MB of text, whereas VARCHAR(20) allows only 20 characters
CHAR(20) stores variable length strings, while VARCHAR(20) pads strings with spaces to 20 bytes
VARCHAR(20) supports unicode characters, while CHAR(20) supports binary data only
questions.explanation: CHAR(n) is fixed-width and right-pads short strings with trailing spaces to 'n' characters. VARCHAR(n) allocates only the necessary bytes for the string length plus overhead bytes.

questions.questionText: What is the evaluated boolean result of the expression 'WHERE status = NULL' in ANSI SQL?
questions.codeSnippet: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE status = NULL;
options: TRUE for all rows where status is NULL
UNKNOWN (Evaluating to NULL/FALSE), returning 0 rows because NULL cannot be compared with '='
TRUE for rows where status contains an empty string ''
FALSE for all rows, but syntax error is thrown
questions.explanation: In SQL 3-valued logic, NULL represents an unknown value. Any equality comparison with NULL (including NULL = NULL) evaluates to UNKNOWN, which resolves to false in WHERE filters. IS NULL must be used instead.

questions.questionText: Which statement accurately describes the difference between TRUNCATE TABLE and DELETE FROM table without a WHERE clause?
options: DELETE is a DDL command that resets identity counters; TRUNCATE is a DML command that logs each row deletion individually
DELETE locks the entire database instance, while TRUNCATE locks only the target row
TRUNCATE is a DDL command that deallocates data pages instantly with minimal logging and resets identity seeds; DELETE is a DML command that deletes rows one by one
TRUNCATE can be executed on tables referenced by active Foreign Keys, while DELETE cannot
questions.explanation: TRUNCATE is a DDL operation that deallocates data pages directly, minimizing transaction log overhead and resetting auto-increment counters. DELETE is DML and logs each deleted tuple individually.

questions.questionText: Which SQL command correctly copies active customer records from the 'prospects' table into the 'customers' table?
options: SELECT INTO customers (name, email) FROM prospects WHERE is_active = 1;
COPY INTO customers FROM prospects WHERE is_active = 1;
UPDATE customers SET (name, email) = (SELECT name, email FROM prospects WHERE is_active = 1);
INSERT INTO customers (name, email) SELECT name, email FROM prospects WHERE is_active = 1;
questions.explanation: The standard ANSI SQL syntax for inserting query results into an existing target table is 'INSERT INTO target_table (cols) SELECT cols FROM source_table WHERE condition'.

questions.questionText: How do UNIQUE constraints differ from PRIMARY KEY constraints in relational databases?
options: PRIMARY KEY constraints allow up to 5 NULL values per table, whereas UNIQUE constraints allow none
A table can have multiple UNIQUE constraints and they allow NULL values (depending on RDBMS standards); a table can have only ONE PRIMARY KEY constraint which strictly forbids NULLs
UNIQUE constraints create clustered indexes automatically, whereas PRIMARY KEY constraints never create indexes
There is no functional difference; UNIQUE and PRIMARY KEY are aliases for the exact same constraint
questions.explanation: A table is limited to one PRIMARY KEY (which automatically enforces NOT NULL). A table can define multiple UNIQUE constraints, which allow NULL values (in standard SQL, multiple NULLs are allowed since NULL != NULL).

questions.questionText: What happens when you execute an ALTER TABLE statement adding a NOT NULL column with a DEFAULT value to a table with 100,000 existing rows?
questions.codeSnippet: ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN tier_level VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'Standard' NOT NULL;
options: The column is added, but only future INSERT statements will receive 'Standard'
The statement fails with an error because existing rows contain NULL for the new column
The column is added and all 100,000 existing rows are populated with the default value 'Standard'
The table is duplicated into a temporary file and existing rows are deleted
questions.explanation: Adding a column with DEFAULT 'Standard' NOT NULL populates all existing rows with 'Standard', satisfying the NOT NULL requirement across the table.

questions.questionText: What will be the result of executing the following UPDATE query?
options: Updates category names to 1.10 in the categories table
Increases the price by 10% for all products belonging to the 'Electronics' category
Fails because subqueries are strictly forbidden inside UPDATE statements
Decreases the price of 'Electronics' products by 10%
questions.explanation: The query uses an IN clause with a scalar subquery to find category IDs named 'Electronics', and increases the matching products' prices by 10% (price * 1.10).

questions.questionText: Which LIKE pattern correctly matches product codes that start with 'AB_', where '_' is a literal underscore character and not a single-character wildcard?
options: WHERE code LIKE 'AB_%'
WHERE code LIKE 'AB\_%' ESCAPE '\'
WHERE code LIKE 'AB*%'
WHERE code LIKE 'AB[1-9]%'
questions.explanation: In SQL LIKE clauses, '_' is a single-character wildcard. To match a literal underscore, it must be escaped (e.g. 'AB\_%') with an explicit ESCAPE '\' declaration.

questions.questionText: What value is returned by COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 'Default Value', 'Secondary Value')?
questions.codeSnippet: SELECT COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 'Default Value', 'Secondary Value') AS result;
options: 'Secondary Value'
'Default Value'
NULL
An array containing both 'Default Value' and 'Secondary Value'
questions.explanation: COALESCE returns the first non-NULL expression in its list of arguments. Here, the first two arguments are NULL, so it evaluates and returns 'Default Value'.

questions.questionText: What error occurs if an application attempts to insert a record into 'orders' with customer_id = 999 when customer_id 999 does not exist in 'customers'?
options: Foreign Key / Referential Integrity Constraint Violation
Deadlock Timeout Exception
Check Constraint Violation
Unique Key Violation
questions.explanation: Inserting a referencing foreign key value that does not exist in the referenced parent table violates Foreign Key (Referential Integrity) constraints.

questions.questionText: Which statement best describes the evaluation of a CHECK constraint on row insertion?
questions.codeSnippet: ALTER TABLE accounts ADD CONSTRAINT chk_balance CHECK (balance >= 0);
options: CHECK constraints are enforced only during DELETE operations
The row is accepted if the expression evaluates to TRUE or UNKNOWN (NULL); it is rejected only if it evaluates to FALSE
The row is accepted only if the expression evaluates strictly to TRUE; NULL balance values trigger an immediate error
CHECK constraints run asynchronously in background cron jobs
questions.explanation: In SQL standards, a CHECK constraint allows the insert/update if the predicate evaluates to TRUE or UNKNOWN (NULL). It fails only if the condition evaluates explicitly to FALSE.

questions.questionText: Which ANSI SQL function extracts the calendar year from a timestamp column named 'created_at'?
questions.codeSnippet: SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM created_at) FROM orders;
options: EXTRACT(YEAR FROM created_at)
YEAROF(created_at)
DATE_TO_YEAR(created_at)
GET_YEAR(created_at)
questions.explanation: The ANSI SQL standard function for extracting sub-fields (such as YEAR, MONTH, DAY) from date/timestamp values is EXTRACT(field FROM timestamp).

questions.questionText: In SQL WHERE clauses, what is the evaluation precedence among NOT, AND, and OR operators?
questions.codeSnippet: SELECT * FROM items WHERE status = 'A' OR status = 'B' AND price < 50;
options: OR is evaluated first, followed by AND, followed by NOT
Left-to-right evaluation regardless of operator keywords
AND and OR have equal precedence and evaluate right-to-left
NOT is evaluated first, followed by AND, followed by OR
questions.explanation: In standard SQL operator precedence: NOT has highest precedence, followed by AND, and finally OR. Parentheses should be used to override default precedence.

questions.questionText: What happens to auto-increment identity sequence values when an INSERT transaction fails and rolls back?
options: The sequence generator rolls back to its previous number, ensuring zero gaps in sequence
The generated sequence number is consumed and lost, leaving a gap in the identity sequence
The database converts the column to a random GUID
The entire database table is locked until a manual sequence repair script is executed
questions.explanation: Sequence generators operate outside of transaction rollback boundaries for performance and concurrency. If an INSERT rolls back, the generated number is discarded, resulting in sequential gaps.

questions.questionText: By default in ANSI SQL, where are NULL values sorted when executing ORDER BY column ASC?
questions.codeSnippet: SELECT name, score FROM students ORDER BY score ASC;
options: NULL values are placed at the beginning or end depending on RDBMS (e.g. PostgreSQL places NULLs last for ASC, MySQL/SQL Server place NULLs first for ASC)
NULL values are discarded from the result set entirely
NULL values cause the query execution to fail with a sorting error
NULL values are automatically converted to zero
questions.explanation: ANSI SQL allows RDBMS implementations to determine default NULL ordering (or explicit NULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST). In PostgreSQL ASC defaults to NULLS LAST, while MySQL/SQL Server place NULLs first.

questions.questionText: When dropping a parent table referenced by foreign keys, what does the RESTRICT option enforce?
questions.codeSnippet: DROP TABLE categories RESTRICT;
options: Deletes only rows that have no matching foreign keys
Converts the table to a temporary read-only state for 24 hours
Drops the parent table and automatically drops all dependent child tables
Aborts the drop operation if any dependent objects or foreign key constraints reference the table
questions.explanation: RESTRICT (the default in SQL standard) blocks the deletion of a schema object if any dependent objects (such as foreign key constraints or views) reference it.

questions.questionText: What will be the output value of the following searched CASE expression when grade = 85?
questions.codeSnippet:
SELECT CASE 
  WHEN grade >= 90 THEN 'A'
  WHEN grade >= 80 THEN 'B'
  WHEN grade >= 70 THEN 'C'
  ELSE 'F'
END AS letter_grade;
options: 'B' and 'C'
questions.explanation: CASE expressions evaluate WHEN conditions sequentially. For grade = 85, the first condition (>= 90) is false, and the second condition (>= 80) is true, returning 'B' immediately.

questions.questionText: Which factor prevents a SQL view from being directly updateable via UPDATE or INSERT operations?
options: The view definition contains aggregate functions (SUM, COUNT), GROUP BY, or DISTINCT clauses
The view contains more than 3 columns
The view definition includes an INNER JOIN between two tables
The view is queried by more than one user concurrently
questions.explanation: Views containing aggregate functions, GROUP BY, DISTINCT, HAVING, or UNION cannot map modified view rows 1-to-1 back to underlying base table rows, rendering them non-updateable.

questions.questionText: What condition must a table satisfy to be in Third Normal Form (3NF)?
options: It must store all data in a single JSON column without indexes
It must be in 2NF and contain no transitive functional dependencies (non-key attributes must depend strictly on the primary key)
It must contain no duplicate rows regardless of primary key definitions
Every column in the table must be a foreign key pointing to another table
questions.explanation: Third Normal Form (3NF) requires the table to be in 2NF and have no transitive dependencies: every non-prime attribute must depend non-transitively directly on the primary key ('the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key').

questions.questionText: Under what condition can a Relational Database Query Optimizer perform an Index-Only Scan to fulfill a SELECT query without fetching table rows from disk heaps?
options: When the database uses SQLite in memory mode exclusively
When the table contains fewer than 100 rows
When all columns requested in the SELECT clause and WHERE filter are contained directly within the B-Tree index itself
When a FULL OUTER JOIN is executed on primary keys
questions.explanation: An Index-Only Scan occurs when a covering index contains all requested query fields (SELECT and WHERE). The engine reads data directly from the index in RAM without disk heap I/O.

questions.questionText: Which SQL Window Function allows a query to access data from the next or previous row in the result set without performing a self-join?
questions.codeSnippet:
SELECT 
    order_date,
    total_amount,
    LAG(total_amount, 1) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS prev_order_amount,
    total_amount - LAG(total_amount, 1) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS diff
FROM orders;
options: LAG() and LEAD()
FIRST_VALUE() and LAST_VALUE()
ROW_NUMBER() and RANK()
NTILE() and CUME_DIST()
questions.explanation: `LAG()` accesses data from a previous row, and `LEAD()` accesses data from a subsequent row relative to the current position within the defined window partition.

questions.questionText: What is the primary usage of a `WITH RECURSIVE` CTE in relational databases?
questions.codeSnippet:
WITH RECURSIVE OrgChart AS (
    SELECT emp_id, name, manager_id, 1 AS level
    FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT e.emp_id, e.name, e.manager_id, o.level + 1
    FROM employees e
    JOIN OrgChart o ON e.manager_id = o.emp_id
)
SELECT * FROM OrgChart;
options: To query hierarchical, tree-structured, or graph network data like organizational charts and bill of materials
To encrypt passwords stored in text columns
To bypass database security permissions and grant superuser access
To automatically create foreign key triggers across multiple databases
questions.explanation: `WITH RECURSIVE` enables traversal of hierarchical or graph-structured datasets (such as parent-child employee org charts, categories, or network paths) by repeatedly executing an anchor query.

questions.questionText: Which ANSI SQL Transaction Isolation level guarantees protection against Dirty Reads, Non-Repeatable Reads, and Phantom Reads?
options: SERIALIZABLE
REPEATABLE READ
READ COMMITTED
READ UNCOMMITTED
questions.explanation: `SERIALIZABLE` is the highest isolation level. It enforces strict transaction execution sequence as if transactions occurred serially, preventing Dirty Reads, Non-Repeatable Reads, and Phantom Reads.

questions.questionText: In SQL Three-Valued Logic (TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN), what is the evaluation result of the expression `SELECT * FROM users WHERE status = NULL;`?
questions.codeSnippet: SELECT * FROM users WHERE status = NULL; -- Returns 0 rows!
options: It returns all rows where status is NULL
It evaluates to UNKNOWN (falsy), returning 0 rows; `IS NULL` must be used instead
It converts NULL to an empty string ''
It raises a SyntaxError during execution
questions.explanation: In SQL, NULL represents an unknown value. Comparisons using `=`, `<>`, or `!=` with NULL evaluate to UNKNOWN, which fails WHERE conditions. Developers must use `IS NULL` or `IS NOT NULL`.

-- Project 1: E-Commerce Sales & Customer Lifetime Value (LTV) Analytics
-- File: ecommerce_analytics.sql

    full_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,

    city VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    joined_date DATE NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS orders (
    order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
    order_date DATE NOT NULL,
    total_amount DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,
    status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('Completed', 'Pending', 'Cancelled')),
    FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(customer_id)
);

-- 2. Populate Sample Dataset

('Bhavana Kolla', 'bhavana@example.com', 'Hyderabad', '2025-02-14'),

INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, order_date, total_amount, status) VALUES
(1, '2025-03-20', 4500.00, 'Completed'),
(1, '2025-04-02', 12500.50, 'Completed'),
(2, '2025-03-22', 8900.00, 'Completed'),

-- 3. Executive Sales Metrics Query (Overall Revenue & AOV)
SELECT 
    COUNT(order_id) AS total_orders,
    SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'Completed' THEN total_amount ELSE 0 END) AS total_revenue,
    ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN status = 'Completed' THEN total_amount END), 2) AS avg_order_value
FROM orders;

-- 4. Customer Lifetime Value (LTV) & VIP Ranking Query
SELECT 
    c.customer_id,
    c.full_name,
    c.city,
    COUNT(o.order_id) AS total_purchases,
    COALESCE(SUM(o.total_amount), 0.00) AS lifetime_value,
    CASE 
        WHEN SUM(o.total_amount) >= 20000 THEN 'VIP Diamond'
        WHEN SUM(o.total_amount) >= 10000 THEN 'Gold Preferred'
        ELSE 'Regular Shopper'
    END AS customer_tier
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id AND o.status = 'Completed'
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.full_name, c.city
HAVING SUM(o.total_amount) > 0
ORDER BY lifetime_value DESC;

WITH DeptStats AS (
    SELECT 
        e.emp_id,
        e.emp_name,
        d.dept_name,
        e.salary,
        AVG(e.salary) OVER (PARTITION BY e.dept_id) AS dept_avg_salary,
        RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY e.dept_id ORDER BY e.salary DESC) AS salary_rank_in_dept

    ROUND(((salary - dept_avg_salary) / dept_avg_salary) * 100, 1) AS pct_above_avg
FROM DeptStats
ORDER BY dept_name, salary_rank_in_dept;

projects.starterCode:
# Project 3: Persistent Library Inventory & Transaction Management System
# File: library_system.py

import sqlite3

class LibraryDatabase:
    def __init__(self, db_path=":memory:"):
        self.conn = sqlite3.connect(db_path)
        self.conn.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;")
        self.cursor = self.conn.cursor()
        self.setup_schema()

    def setup_schema(self):
        # 1. Books Table
        self.cursor.execute('''
            CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS books (
                book_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
                title TEXT NOT NULL,
                author TEXT NOT NULL,
                total_copies INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK(total_copies >= 0),
                available_copies INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK(available_copies >= 0)
            );
        ''')

        # 2. Borrow Log Table
        self.cursor.execute('''
            CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS borrow_log (
                log_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
                book_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
                member_name TEXT NOT NULL,
                borrow_date DATE DEFAULT (DATE('now')),
                return_date DATE,
                FOREIGN KEY (book_id) REFERENCES books(book_id)
            );
        ''')

        # 3. View for Active Loans
        self.cursor.execute('''
            CREATE VIEW IF NOT EXISTS v_active_loans AS
            SELECT 
                l.log_id,
                b.title,
                b.author,
                l.member_name,
                l.borrow_date
            FROM borrow_log l
            JOIN books b ON l.book_id = b.book_id
            WHERE l.return_date IS NULL;
        ''')

        # 4. Insert Initial Books
        self.cursor.executemany('''
            INSERT INTO books (title, author, total_copies, available_copies)
            VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)
        ''', [
            ("SQL & Relational Database Mastery", "Siddharth Nair", 5, 5),
            ("Python for Data Analysis", "Charles Severance", 3, 3),
            ("Designing Data-Intensive Applications", "Martin Kleppmann", 2, 2)
        ])
        self.conn.commit()

    def borrow_book(self, book_id, member_name):
        """Executes borrow workflow in an ACID Compliant Transaction"""
        try:
            self.cursor.execute("BEGIN TRANSACTION;")
            
            # Check availability
            self.cursor.execute("SELECT available_copies, title FROM books WHERE book_id = ?", (book_id,))
            row = self.cursor.fetchone()
            
            if not row:
                raise ValueError("Book ID not found.")
            
            available, title = row
            if available <= 0:
                raise ValueError(f"No copies of '{title}' currently available!")

            # Log borrow event
            self.cursor.execute('''
                INSERT INTO borrow_log (book_id, member_name)
                VALUES (?, ?)
            ''', (book_id, member_name))

            # Deduct inventory
            self.cursor.execute('''
                UPDATE books SET available_copies = available_copies - 1
                WHERE book_id = ?
            ''', (book_id,))

            self.conn.commit()
            print(f"✓ Successfully borrowed '{title}' for {member_name}.")
            return True

        except Exception as e:
            self.conn.rollback()
            print(f"✗ Transaction Aborted: {e}")
            return False

    def display_active_loans(self):
        self.cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM v_active_loans;")
        rows = self.cursor.fetchall()
        print("\n=== CURRENT ACTIVE LIBRARY LOANS ===")
        print(f"{'ID':<4} {'Title':<35} {'Member':<15} {'Borrow Date':<12}")
        print("-" * 70)
        for r in rows:
            print(f"{r[0]:<4} {r[1]:<35} {r[3]:<15} {r[4]:<12}")
        print("-" * 70)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    lib = LibraryDatabase()
    lib.borrow_book(1, "Arshith Kumar")
    lib.borrow_book(1, "Bhavana Kolla")
    lib.borrow_book(2, "Chandan Verma")
    lib.display_active_loans()

readingMaterial.introduction: Welcome to modern full-stack web development! Every digital interaction on the web — from social networking and streaming platforms to cloud banking and e-commerce portals — is powered by a globally distributed network architecture. In this foundational module, you will learn the core engineering principles of how the internet transmits information, how domain names resolve to physical IP addresses, how clients and servers communicate over HTTP/HTTPS, how web browser engines parse and render pages, and how professional software developers configure tools like VS Code and Chrome DevTools.
objectives: Differentiate between static informational websites and dynamic, distributed web applications
Deconstruct the Client-Server architecture and the OSI/TCP-IP networking model
Trace the complete lifecycle of a domain request from browser address bar to server response
Master HTTP/HTTPS protocol mechanics: Request methods, response status codes, and HTTP headers
Understand DNS hierarchy: Root servers, TLD name servers, authoritative name servers, and records
Explore web browser internal architecture: Networking, HTML parser, CSS parser, DOM/CSSOM tree, and rendering engine
Configure a professional local web development environment with VS Code and browser Developer Tools

terminology.definition: A device or user-agent software application (such as Chrome, Safari, or a mobile app) that requests resources from a centralized server across a computer network.
A high-performance computer system or software daemon listening on a network port, designed to process client requests and serve data, files, or services.
A unique numerical identifier assigned to every device connected to a computer network (e.g., IPv4 32-bit: 192.168.1.1; IPv6 128-bit: 2001:0db8:85a3::8a2e:0370:7334).
The hierarchical decentralized naming system that acts as the phonebook of the internet, translating human-friendly domain names (e.g., google.com) into machine-routable IP addresses.
HyperText Transfer Protocol (and its TLS/SSL encrypted counterpart), the stateless application-layer communication protocol governing web data exchange.
A geographically distributed network of proxy cache servers that deliver web content (images, styles, scripts) with minimal latency to nearby users.
An in-memory, tree-structured programmatic representation of an HTML document created by the browser engine for script interaction.

sections.heading: 1. Websites vs. Web Applications: Architectural Differences
sections.text: The web has evolved through distinct eras: from static document publishing (Web 1.0) to dynamic interactive user-generated platforms (Web 2.0), and modern decentralized cloud apps. Understanding the difference between static websites and dynamic web applications is critical for selecting appropriate architectural patterns.
bulletPoints: Static Websites: Deliver pre-rendered HTML, CSS, and asset files directly to the client. The server does not alter files dynamically before transmission. Examples: Portfolios, documentation sites, landing pages.

Dynamic Web Applications: Run backend business logic (Node.js, Python, Java) connected to databases (PostgreSQL, MongoDB). Content is assembled per-user on demand. Examples: Netflix, Gmail, Amazon, Trello.
Single-Page Applications (SPAs): Load a solitary HTML document and dynamically update the DOM view via client-side JavaScript execution without full-page browser refreshes.

sections.heading: 2. The Complete Request-Response Lifecycle: From Keystroke to Pixels
sections.text: When an engineer understands exactly what transpires between typing a URL into the browser omnibox and seeing the rendered pixels, troubleshooting production networking bottlenecks becomes second nature.
bulletPoints: Step 1: URL Parsing & HSTS Check: The browser parses the protocol (https), domain (arshithbootcamp.com), port (:443), and path. It checks the preloaded HSTS list to force secure HTTPS.
Step 2: DNS Resolution Chain: Checks browser DNS cache -> OS cache (/etc/hosts) -> Router DNS -> ISP Recursive Resolver -> Root Server -> TLD Server (.com) -> Authoritative Nameserver.
Step 3: TCP Connection (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK): Establishes reliable point-to-point byte stream over port 443.
Step 4: TLS 1.3 Handshake: Client and server exchange cryptographic keys, verify SSL certificates, and establish end-to-end symmetric AES encryption.
Step 5: HTTP Transmission: Client transmits request headers (User-Agent, Accept, Cookie). Server processes and streams response code (200 OK), Content-Type, and HTML payload.

Step 6: Critical Rendering Path (CRP): Browser tokenizes HTML into DOM nodes, parses stylesheets into CSSOM, combines them into a Render Tree, computes Layout (geometry), and Paints pixels to the viewport.

rows: Request received, protocol upgrade in progress (e.g., WebSockets)

Further action needed; resource moved or cached copy valid

Malformed request, missing credentials, or invalid resource URI
500 Internal Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Unavailable, 504 Gateway Timeout
Server crashed, unhandled exception, or upstream gateway failure

sections.heading: 3. DNS Infrastructure & Domain Configuration
sections.text: Domain names are human-memorable aliases for IP addresses. DNS records tell internet routers where to direct traffic for web servers, email exchanges, and domain verification.
bulletPoints: A Record (Address): Maps a domain name directly to an IPv4 address (e.g., example.com -> 93.184.216.34).
AAAA Record: Maps a domain name to an IPv6 address (128-bit hexadecimal).
CNAME (Canonical Name): Maps an alias domain to another domain name (e.g., www.example.com -> example.com).
MX Record (Mail Exchange): Directs inbound email to corporate mail servers (e.g., Google Workspace, Microsoft 365).
TXT Record: Carries machine-readable text used for domain verification, SPF (Sender Policy Framework), and DKIM security.

sections.heading: 4. Browser Internals & DevTools Mastering
sections.text: Modern browsers (Chromium, Gecko, WebKit) are complex operating systems in their own right. Mastering Developer Tools (F12 or Ctrl+Shift+I) transforms debugging from guesswork into scientific analysis.
bulletPoints: Elements Panel: Live inspect and modify DOM tree nodes, CSS cascade rules, box-model dimensions, and pseudo-classes (:hover, :focus).
Console Panel: REPL for JavaScript execution, interactive logging (console.log, console.table, console.error), and uncaught exception stack traces.
Network Panel: Real-time telemetry of all HTTP requests: waterfall timeline, status codes, payload sizes, MIME types, request headers, cookies, and network throttling (simulate Slow 3G).
Application Panel: Inspect browser storage: LocalStorage, SessionStorage, Cookies, IndexedDB, Cache Storage, and Service Workers.

modules.title: Module 02: HTML5 — Web Page Structure
modules.description: Semantic HTML tags, document structure, head metadata, typography, links, lists, accessibility, and SEO foundations.

readingMaterial.introduction: HyperText Markup Language (HTML5) is the structural skeleton of the World Wide Web. Every webpage you view is an HTML document parsed by the browser engine into a hierarchical Document Object Model (DOM) tree. In this module, you will learn to construct robust, semantic, accessible, and SEO-friendly document architectures using modern HTML5 standards. We examine core elements, heading hierarchies, text formatting, hyperlinks, document metadata, and accessibility (a11y) landmarks.
objectives: Master the syntactic rules of HTML5 elements, attributes, and void tags
Construct a valid HTML5 document skeleton from <!DOCTYPE html> to closing </html>
Configure rich metadata in the <head> element for responsive design, SEO, and Open Graph previews
Implement proper semantic tags: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <section>, <aside>, and <footer>
Structure accessible heading hierarchies (h1 through h6) without skipping levels
Create complex nested lists (ordered, unordered, description) and hyperlinks with security attributes
Apply Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) principles including ARIA landmarks and screen reader support

terminology.definition:
A complete individual component of an HTML document, consisting of an opening tag, optional attributes, content, and a closing tag (e.g.,

Hello

).

An HTML tag that cannot contain child content or a closing tag, such as ,
,
, , and .
A name-value pair placed inside an opening tag that configures behavior or metadata for the element (e.g., href='...', id='...', alt='...').
Markup that conveys human- and machine-readable meaning about its content rather than merely defining its visual presentation.
The living tree data structure constructed by the browser engine representing the HTML document in memory.
The practice of designing websites usable by people with disabilities, including screen reader users, keyboard-only users, and those with visual impairments.

sections.heading: 1. The Anatomy of an HTML5 Element & Document Skeleton
sections.text: HTML elements consist of opening tags, element content, and closing tags. Case-insensitivity exists historically, but lowercase syntax is the universal industry standard.
bulletPoints: <!DOCTYPE html>: Tells modern browsers to render in standards-compliant mode rather than quirks mode.
<html lang='en'>: Root element declaring the primary human language of the document for screen readers and search crawlers.
<head>: Machine-readable container for metadata, stylesheets, title, fonts, and scripts not rendered directly in the viewport.
<body>: Container for all user-visible content rendered on screen.

rows: Introductory content / banner for page or section
Defines 'navigation' landmark; keyboard shortcuts jump here
Dominant unique content of the document
Defines 'main' landmark; allows 'Skip to content' links
Assists RSS readers and syndication parsers
Defines 'complementary' landmark; easily bypassed by a11y tools
Footer for its nearest section or root document
Defines 'contentinfo' landmark with metadata & legal terms

sections.heading: 2. Head Metadata, SEO, and Open Graph Protocols
sections.text: The <head> element houses metadata that directly affects search engine rankings, social media link previews, and mobile viewport responsiveness.
bulletPoints: <meta charset='UTF-8'>: Specifies the standard character encoding supporting almost all human languages and emoji symbols.
<meta name='viewport' content='width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0'>: Essential tag instructing mobile devices to scale width to screen width and initialize 1:1 scale.
<meta name='description' content='...'>: The summary snippet displayed in search engine result pages (SERPs).
Open Graph Tags (og:title, og:image, og:description): Dictate the rich card preview generated when links are shared on LinkedIn, Twitter, Discord, and WhatsApp.

sections.heading: 3. Hyperlinks and File Path Resolution
sections.text: Hyperlinks (<a>) interconnect the web. Understanding path resolution prevents broken links across development and production environments.
bulletPoints: Absolute URLs: Full protocol and domain path (e.g. href='https://example.com/docs'). Used for external domains.
Root-Relative URLs: Path starting with a forward slash (e.g. href='/about'). Resolves relative to domain root.
Document-Relative URLs: Path relative to current file location (e.g. href='./sub/page.html' or href='../index.html').
Security Attribute: When opening new windows with target='_blank', always include rel='noopener noreferrer' to prevent window.opener phishing exploits and improve performance.

readingMaterial.introduction: Forms and multimedia turn static web pages into interactive, immersive applications. Forms are the primary interface for collecting user input — enabling authentication, search queries, transactions, and file uploads. Modern HTML5 also provides native multimedia elements (<audio>, <video>, <picture>) that eliminate legacy plugins (like Flash) and deliver performant, responsive media across all device form factors.
objectives: Architect accessible HTML forms using <form>, <fieldset>, <legend>, and <label>
Select appropriate HTML5 input types (email, password, number, tel, date, range, file)
Implement native browser form validation using HTML5 Constraint Validation attributes
Differentiate between GET and POST form submission methods and encode types (enctype)
Embed performant, accessible images using responsive <picture>, srcset, and sizes attributes
Deliver native audio and video with custom controls, captions (<track>), and autoplay policies
Securely embed third-party widgets and video players using responsive <iframe> and sandbox

terminology.definition: action specifies the target URL endpoint receiving data; method specifies the HTTP transfer verb (GET appends params to URL query string; POST sends data in request body).
Browser-native JavaScript and HTML mechanism to test form validity before sending data to the server (e.g. required, pattern, min/max).
Serving differently cropped, composed, or scaled image files based on device viewport characteristics using the <picture> element.
Two-part identifier for file formats transmitted over the internet (e.g., image/webp, video/mp4, application/json).
Security attribute on <iframe> that restricts capabilities (scripts, forms, popups, same-origin access) of embedded third-party pages.

sections.heading: 1. Form Architecture: Labels, Grouping, and Accessibility
sections.text: Accessible form design requires pairing every interactive input control with an explicitly associated <label>. Using the 'for' attribute matching the input's 'id' expands clickable touch targets and gives screen readers critical context.
bulletPoints: <form action='/api/login' method='POST'>: Container defining the submission endpoint and HTTP method.
<label for='user-email'>: Associates accessible label with input id='user-email'. Clicking label focuses the input.
<fieldset> and <legend>: Groups related form inputs (e.g., Billing Address, Shipping Preferences) semantically.
ARIA attributes (aria-describedby, aria-invalid): Links error text messages to invalid form inputs.

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                    HTML5 FORM ARCHITECTURE & DATA FLOW                |
|                                                                       |
|   <form action="/api/checkout" method="POST" enctype="...">           |
|      +-------------------------------------------------------------+  |
|      | <fieldset>                                                  |  |
|      |   <legend>Payment Information</legend>                      |  |
|      |                                                             |  |
|      |   <label for="card-num">Credit Card Number</label>          |  |
|      |   <input id="card-num" type="text" required pattern="\d{16}">|
|      |                                                             |  |
|      |   <label for="exp">Expiry Date</label>                      |  |
|      |   <input id="exp" type="month" required>                    |  |
|      +-------------------------------------------------------------+  |
|      | <button type="submit">Complete Purchase</button>            |  |
|      +-------------------------------------------------------------+  |
|                                                                       |
|  Client Browser Validates Inputs -> Encodes Payload -> HTTP POST ->   |
|  Server API Endpoint Validates -> Stores in DB -> Returns JSON/HTML   |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+

sections.heading: 2. Form Submission Methods: GET vs. POST vs. multipart/form-data
sections.text: Selecting the correct HTTP method and encoding type is critical for data security and server processing.
bulletPoints: GET Method: Encodes form values as URL query string parameters (e.g., /search?q=web+development). Ideal for search filters and bookmarks. Never use for passwords or payment data.
POST Method: Encodes form values within the HTTP request body. Supports large payloads and conceals data from browser history and server access logs.
application/x-www-form-urlencoded: Default POST encoding converting characters to key=value pairs separated by '&'.
multipart/form-data: Mandatory encoding when uploading files (<input type='file'>); divides payload into distinct binary MIME parts.

sections.heading: 3. Responsive Images & Art Direction with <picture>
sections.text: Serving modern, responsive images is the single highest-impact optimization for mobile web performance. The <picture> element and srcset attribute prevent mobile devices from downloading giant desktop images.
bulletPoints: srcset and sizes: Allows the browser to choose the most appropriate image resolution based on display pixel density and viewport width.
element: Wraps multiple elements and an fallback, allowing art direction (serving different crops for mobile vs desktop) and modern format fallbacks (AVIF -> WebP -> JPEG).

modules.title: Module 04: CSS Fundamentals & Styling
modules.description: Cascading style sheets, selectors, specificity hierarchy, box model, border-box, typography, colors, and CSS custom properties.

readingMaterial.introduction: Cascading Style Sheets (CSS3) is the visual styling engine of the open web. CSS dictates how HTML elements are formatted, positioned, animated, and adapted across screens. In this module, you will master the foundational mechanics of CSS: the cascade algorithm, selector specificity hierarchy, the box model, margin collapse, font metrics, color systems, and modern CSS custom properties (variables) for scalable design systems and dark-mode theming.
objectives: Understand the CSS Cascade algorithm, inheritance rules, and the specificity scoring model
Apply complex CSS selectors: combinators, attribute selectors, pseudo-classes, and pseudo-elements
Master the CSS Box Model: content, padding, border, margin, and box-sizing: border-box
Explain and resolve vertical margin collapsing behavior
Implement fluid typography using clamp(), rem, em, and web font loading strategies
Utilize modern color spaces: Hex, RGB/RGBA, HSL/HSLA, and color-mix()
Architect design systems using CSS Custom Properties (CSS variables) for dynamic dark mode themes

terminology.definition: The algorithm used by CSS engines to resolve conflicts when multiple styling rules target the same HTML element, based on origin, specificity, and source order.
A 4-part weight score (Inline, IDs, Classes/Pseudo-classes/Attributes, Elements/Pseudo-elements) determining which CSS declaration takes precedence.
The fundamental geometry model of every HTML element, comprised of the core content box surrounded by padding, border, and margin layers.
The industry-standard CSS rule that includes padding and borders inside an element's declared width and height, preventing layout breakage.
The behavior where adjacent vertical margins combine into a single margin equal to the largest of the two rather than adding together.
Author-defined entities (prefixed with --) that store reusable values accessed via var() and dynamically inherited through the cascade.

sections.heading: 1. The Cascade, Specificity Hierarchy, and Inheritance
sections.text: When multiple CSS declarations target the same element, the browser cascade algorithm determines the winner using a strict priority order: 1) Importance (!important), 2) Origin (User Agent vs User vs Author), 3) Specificity Score, 4) Source Order (later rules override earlier rules).
bulletPoints: Inline Styles: Written directly on element (style='...') -> Specificity: 1-0-0-0.
ID Selectors: Targeting #submit-btn -> Specificity: 0-1-0-0.
Class, Attribute, and Pseudo-classes: Targeting .btn, [type='submit'], :hover -> Specificity: 0-0-1-0.
Element and Pseudo-elements: Targeting button, div, ::before -> Specificity: 0-0-0-1.
Universal Selector (*): Specificity score of 0-0-0-0; contributes zero specificity weight.
sections.diagram:
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                    CSS SPECIFICITY CALCULATION MATRIX                 |
|                                                                       |
|  [ Inline Styles ] -> Weight: 1,0,0,0  (e.g., style="color: red")     |
|         v                                                             |
|  [ ID Selectors ]  -> Weight: 0,1,0,0  (e.g., #primary-nav)           |
|         v                                                             |
|  [ Classes / Pseudo-classes / Attributes ] -> Weight: 0,0,1,0         |
|                       (e.g., .card, :hover, [type="text"])            |
|         v                                                             |
|  [ Elements & Pseudo-elements ] -> Weight: 0,0,0,1                    |
|                       (e.g., h1, div, p, ::before)                    |
|                                                                       |
|  Example Calculation:                                                 |
|  nav.navbar ul.menu li a:hover                                        |
|  = 3 classes/pseudo (.navbar, .menu, :hover) = 0,0,3,0                |
|  + 4 elements (nav, ul, li, a)              = 0,0,0,4                |
|  Total Specificity = 0-0-3-4                                          |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+

sections.heading: 2. The CSS Box Model & box-sizing: border-box
sections.text: Every rendered HTML element is a rectangular box. By default in CSS (content-box), setting width: 300px only sets the inner content area. Adding 20px padding and 5px border expands the rendered box width to 350px. Setting box-sizing: border-box forces padding and border inside the declared width.
bulletPoints: Content: Where text and images render.
Padding: Transparent space between content and the border.
Border: Visible boundary line enclosing content and padding.
Margin: Transparent space outside the border separating the element from neighbors.
Universal Reset: Apply *, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; } to all stylesheets.

sections.heading: 3. CSS Custom Properties (Variables) & Theming Architecture
sections.text: CSS variables enable modular, maintainable stylesheets. Declared on the :root pseudo-class, custom properties inherit throughout the entire DOM tree.
bulletPoints: Declaration Syntax: Prefixed with two dashes (e.g., --color-brand: #10b981;).
Access Syntax: Retrieved via var(--color-brand, #fallback).
Dynamic Theming: Changing variables inside a [data-theme='dark'] selector instantly updates all dependent components without duplicating CSS rules.

keyTakeaways: The CSS Cascade resolves conflicting declarations using importance, specificity score, and source order.
The universal box-sizing: border-box rule ensures padding and borders are included in calculated element dimensions.
Adjacent vertical margins collapse in normal flow, a behavior eliminated by flexbox and grid formatting contexts.
CSS Custom Properties (--variable) empower dynamic runtime theme switching and maintainable design systems.
Relative length units (rem and em) preserve typography scalability and accessibility when users adjust font sizes.
